report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **oversimplified and not well supported as a blanket statement**. Rigorous evidence shows vegetarian diets can *reduce risk of certain causes of death* (especially ischemic heart disease) but do **not** reliably increase overall life expectancy or reduce all-cause mortality compared with omnivorous diets when nutrient adequacy is considered.

**Evidence:**

1. A 2021 meta-analysis of vegetarian vs. non-vegetarian diets found reduced ischemic heart disease mortality, but **no significant effect on all-cause or cerebrovascular mortality**, with the authors noting low certainty of evidence (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/).

2. The large EPIC-Oxford cohort study—one of the most rigorous UK prospective studies—found **no significant difference in all-cause mortality** between vegetarians and meat-eaters (death rate ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.86–1.27, not statistically significant) (https://www.bdi.ox.ac.uk/publications/7964).

3. A 2026 study covered by ScienceDaily, following over 5,000 people aged 80+, found vegetarians were **~30% less likely to reach age 100** than meat-eaters, though those who included fish, dairy, or eggs fared as well as meat-eaters—suggesting nutrient completeness, not meat-avoidance per se, matters most (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/02/260225081214.htm).

4. A comprehensive 2025 review ("Vegetarian diets for longevity: friend or foe?") concludes evidence is mixed, with benefits for cardiovascular disease but potential risks (nutrient deficiencies, fracture risk) that could offset longevity gains in some populations (https://www.maturitas.org/article/S0378-5122(25)00519-5/fulltext).

**Bottom line:** Vegetarian diets are associated with lower cardiovascular mortality, but claims of increased overall life expectancy versus meat-eating are not consistently supported by high-quality cohort data; effects depend heavily on diet quality and nutrient adequacy, not meat-avoidance alone.
